title: Haggai 2:10–19
context: Haggai’s third oracle is dated to the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month in the second year of Darius (2:10). The LORD tells Haggai to ask the priests for a ruling: holy meat carried in a garment does not make other food holy, but one unclean by contact with a dead body makes what he touches unclean (2:12–13; compare Numbers 19:11 and 19:22). Haggai applies the ruling: “So is this people, and so is this nation before me” (2:14). The LORD recalls the lean harvests and the blight, mildew, and hail of the time before work on the temple began (2:15–17), asks the people to consider “from this day and backward” (2:15, 2:18), and promises, “From today I will bless you” (2:19). Ezra 3:10–11 records a foundation laid earlier, and Haggai 2:18 links the laying of the temple’s foundation with this date; each account can be read in its own place. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as teaching that holiness is not passed on by contact while uncleanness spreads, and that the LORD’s blessing is his gift to a people returning to him.

verses.text: In the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, the LORD’s word came by Haggai the prophet, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The date, “In the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius”, introduces Haggai’s third oracle. Arminian readers note that the LORD continues to speak to the people as the work goes on, guiding them by his word at each stage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s ongoing care for his people through his prophet, with each dated word marking a step in the rebuilding. Shared ground: both traditions read the heading as belonging to the oracle that follows, three months after work began in 1:14–15, and as fixing it in real history.

verses.text: “The LORD of Armies says: Ask now the priests concerning the law, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies tells Haggai, “Ask now the priests concerning the law”. Arminian readers note that the LORD uses the priests’ own teaching to instruct the people, so that they can see the point for themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD honoring the priests’ role as teachers of the law, and using their ruling as the basis for his word. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the law gives the framework for understanding the people’s condition, and that the priests carry real responsibility to teach it.

verses.text: ‘If someone carries holy meat in the fold of his garment, and with his fold touches bread, stew, wine, oil, or any food, will it become holy?’ ” The priests answered, “No.”
verses.arminianNotes: Haggai asks whether holy meat carried “in the fold of his garment” makes other food holy, and the priests answer, “No.” Arminian readers hear the point that holiness is not passed on by mere contact.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the ruling as teaching that holy things do not make other things holy by touch. Shared ground: both traditions read the question as preparing for the application in 2:14, and as showing that the people’s nearness to the altar did not by itself make their lives or work holy.

verses.text: Then Haggai said, “If one who is unclean by reason of a dead body touches any of these, will it be unclean?” The priests answered, “It will be unclean.”
verses.arminianNotes: Haggai asks whether one “who is unclean by reason of a dead body” makes food unclean, and the priests answer, “It will be unclean.” Arminian readers hear the sobering contrast with 2:12: uncleanness spreads more easily than holiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see uncleanness passing by contact, as the law teaches (compare Numbers 19:22). Shared ground: both traditions read the two rulings together as a parable about the people, with the contagion of uncleanness standing in contrast to the holiness that cannot be passed on by touch.

verses.text: Then Haggai answered, “ ‘So is this people, and so is this nation before me,’ says the LORD; ‘and so is every work of their hands. That which they offer there is unclean.
verses.arminianNotes: Haggai applies the ruling as the LORD’s word: “So is this people, and so is this nation before me”. Arminian readers hear a call to see that their offerings were unclean because their lives were not right, and to turn fully to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD declaring that “every work of their hands” was unclean, since outward worship cannot cleanse an unclean people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the people need more than ritual activity; they need the LORD’s cleansing and a renewed relationship with him.

verses.text: Now, please consider from this day and backward, before a stone was laid on a stone in the LORD’s temple.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Now, please consider from this day and backward, before a stone was laid on a stone in the LORD’s temple.” Arminian readers hear an invitation to compare the time of neglect with the time of renewed obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD directing the people’s memory, so that they recognize his hand in their past hardship. Shared ground: both traditions read the call to “consider” as echoing 1:5 and 1:7, and as preparing for the promise of blessing in 2:19 by contrasting the time before the work began.

verses.text: Through all that time, when one came to a heap of twenty measures, there were only ten. When one came to the wine vat to draw out fifty, there were only twenty.
verses.arminianNotes: “Through all that time, when one came to a heap of twenty measures, there were only ten.” Arminian readers hear the LORD reminding the people of disappointments they had felt firsthand, which were meant to turn them back to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s providence in the shortfall of grain and wine, as in 1:6 and 1:9. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recalling the period of neglect, and they read it within this covenant setting rather than as a general rule that measures blessing by harvest size.

verses.text: I struck you with blight, mildew, and hail in all the work of your hands; yet you didn’t turn to me,’ says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I struck you with blight, mildew, and hail in all the work of your hands; yet you didn’t turn to me”. Arminian readers hear a lament over discipline that did not bring the people back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s discipline and the people’s failure to respond, echoing the refrain of Amos 4:9. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that hardship alone does not produce repentance, and that the LORD’s purpose in discipline is that his people turn to him.

verses.text: ‘Consider, please, from this day and backward, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, since the day that the foundation of the LORD’s temple was laid, consider it.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Consider, please, from this day and backward, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month”. Arminian readers hear a call to mark this day as a turning point, now that the people have begun to obey.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD fixing a day from which his blessing will be visible, tied to the day “that the foundation of the LORD’s temple was laid”. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking the people’s renewed work with the LORD’s promised favor, and they read Ezra 3:10–11 in its own place.

verses.text: Is the seed yet in the barn? Yes, the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree haven’t produced. From today I will bless you.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks, “Is the seed yet in the barn?” and then promises, “From today I will bless you.” Arminian readers hear grace that meets the people’s renewed obedience, given before any harvest could prove it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a free promise of blessing that rests on the LORD’s word, not on the people’s merit, since the trees “haven’t produced” yet. Shared ground: both traditions read the promise as the LORD’s gift to a returning people, to be received by faith before it can be seen.
